title: Why non linearity is the whole trick
story:
Here is the fact the whole field rests on, stated as plainly as it can be: composing linear functions gives a linear function.

Apply a weighted sum to some inputs, then apply another weighted sum to those results, then another. However many times you do it, the relationship between the original inputs and the final output is a weighted sum of the original inputs. There exists a single layer that computes precisely the same thing. Not approximately, not for most inputs — exactly, for every input.

So a deep network made only of weighted sums is not a deep network. It is a single layer with an expensive implementation and a much larger number of parameters, all of which are redundant. The depth is not doing less than you hoped; it is doing nothing.

Put a non-linear function between the layers and that collapse stops being available. The composition is no longer expressible as one weighted sum, so the second layer is operating on something the first layer produced rather than on a rearrangement of the inputs. Depth begins to buy expressiveness, and every subsequent layer buys more.

What it buys is worth describing concretely, because the usual phrasing — more capacity, richer features — is vague enough to be unhelpful. Each layer applies a boundary and then bends the space. The next layer applies a boundary in the bent space, which corresponds to a curved or piecewise boundary in the original space. Stack enough of these and the boundary in the original space can be shaped almost arbitrarily. A single flat cut, applied repeatedly to a space that is folded between cuts, produces something no single flat cut could.

That is why the standard example of a function no single unit can compute is solved by adding one layer. Nothing about the boundary-drawing changed. The space it is drawn in changed, because a non-linear step was applied first.

Note what this means about the choice of function, since the choice gets more attention than it deserves. Almost any function that is not a straight line will do for making depth meaningful. Which one you pick affects how easily gradients move through a deep stack during training, how quickly it computes, and whether units can get stuck producing the same output regardless of input. Those are real engineering concerns and they matter for training large models. They are not the reason the function is there. The reason is the collapse, and any non-linear function prevents it.

The limitation to hold alongside all this is that expressiveness is not learnability. Having established that a deep network with non-linear steps can represent an enormous range of functions, you have said nothing about whether training will find the one you want. A structure being able to express your answer and a procedure being able to locate it are different claims, and most practical difficulty lives in the gap. The theoretical results about what these networks can represent are consequently much stronger than anything known about what training reliably achieves — which is worth remembering whenever an argument from expressiveness is offered as a reason something should work.

problem.name: The collapse
problem.shape: Layers are being stacked in the hope that depth adds capability.
tell: a deep stack performs no better than a shallow one
no non-linear step sits between the layers
an argument for a design rests only on what it can represent
the choice of activation is being treated as the source of depth's value
problem.move: Check that a non-linear step sits between every pair of layers, because without one the entire stack collapses to a single layer exactly. Then stop arguing from expressiveness, since being able to represent an answer says nothing about a procedure finding it.
problem.invariant: Composing linear functions gives a linear function, so any stack of weighted sums has a single-layer equivalent that computes the same thing for every input.
problem.breaks: Expressiveness is not learnability. A deep network with non-linear steps can represent an enormous range of functions, and that establishes nothing about whether training will find the one you want — the theory about representation is far stronger than anything known about what training reliably achieves.

cost.time: the non-linear step is computed at every unit of every layer, and the choice affects how well gradients traverse a deep stack
cost.space: none beyond the parameters depth already requires
cost.beats: a single wide layer, which needs no depth and must express everything with one flat boundary, and hand-built features, which impose the curvature yourself and require knowing what curvature is needed

problem.practice: Write two weighted sums on paper with small numbers, compose them by substituting the first into the second, and collect the terms. The result is one weighted sum — that is the collapse, and doing it once makes the argument permanent.

beats.broke: A stack of weighted sums has an exact single-layer equivalent, so a deep network built only from them is a wide network with redundant parameters and depth that does nothing at all.
beats.fix: Insert a non-linear step between layers, which makes the composition inexpressible as one weighted sum — so each layer draws a boundary in a space the previous layer bent.
beats.cost: The non-linear step runs at every unit of every layer, and its choice governs how well gradients traverse a deep stack — though any non-linear function prevents the collapse.

interview.q: Why does a network of stacked weighted sums gain nothing from depth, and what does a non-linear step change?
interview.trap: Answering that depth helps less than expected. It helps exactly zero: there is a single layer computing the identical function for every input, so the parameters are redundant rather than inefficient.
interview.answer:
Because composing linear functions gives a linear function, so the stack has an exact single-layer equivalent.

Apply a weighted sum, then another, then another; the relationship between the original inputs and the final output remains a weighted sum of the original inputs, and one layer computes precisely the same thing — exactly, for every input. So a deep network of weighted sums is a single layer with an expensive implementation and a large number of redundant parameters. The depth is not doing less than hoped, it is doing nothing.

A non-linear function between layers removes the collapse, because the composition can no longer be written as one weighted sum — the second layer operates on something the first produced rather than a rearrangement of the inputs.

Concretely, each layer draws a boundary and bends the space; the next draws a boundary in the bent space, which is a curved or piecewise boundary back in the original one. Stack enough and the boundary can be shaped almost arbitrarily — one flat cut, applied repeatedly to a space folded between cuts, gives something no flat cut could. That is why the standard function no single unit can compute becomes solvable by adding one layer: the boundary-drawing did not change, the space it is drawn in did.

On the choice of function: almost any non-straight-line function makes depth meaningful. The choice affects how gradients move through a deep stack, how fast it computes, and whether units get stuck emitting a constant — real concerns, but not the reason the function is there. The reason is the collapse.

And the limitation I would insist on: expressiveness is not learnability. That such a network can represent an enormous range of functions says nothing about whether training finds the one you want. The theory about representation is far stronger than anything known about what training reliably achieves, which makes an argument from expressiveness weak evidence that something will work.
